reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Amblyopia is reduced best-corrected visual acuity in one or both eyes due to abnormal visual development, in the absence of a structural cause that fully explains the deficit

The main types are strabismic (from ocular misalignment), anisometropic or refractive (from unequal or high refractive error), and stimulus deprivation (from media opacity such as congenital cataract or ptosis)
It develops only during the sensitive period of visual development in early childhood, which is why early detection through vision screening is critical
It is usually unilateral but can be bilateral, for example with high symmetrical refractive error or bilateral media opacity
A crowding phenomenon is characteristic, with worse acuity for lines of letters than for single optotypes
Deprivation amblyopia from causes such as congenital cataract is the most severe and least responsive type and needs urgent treatment
Management is to correct any refractive error and to treat the underlying cause, then to encourage use of the amblyopic eye with occlusion (patching) or pharmacological penalisation of the better eye
Treatment is most effective when started young; response diminishes with increasing age although some improvement can still occur in older children
reference.pathophysiology: Amblyopia results from abnormal visual experience during the critical period of cortical visual development. When the two eyes receive unequal or degraded input (from misalignment, unequal refractive error, or media opacity), competitive cortical mechanisms favour the better eye and suppress the input from the affected eye. This leads to persistent cortical under-development of that eye's pathway and reduced acuity that is not correctable by optical means alone once the sensitive period has passed, though it remains treatable if addressed early.
additionalDifferentials: Structural ocular disease (e.g. optic nerve or macular pathology) causing reduced vision
Retinoblastoma or other intraocular tumour presenting with poor vision
additionalInvestigations: Age-appropriate best-corrected visual acuity testing, ideally with crowded (linear) optotypes
Cycloplegic refraction to detect anisometropia or significant refractive error
Cover testing and motility assessment to detect associated strabismus
Dilated fundus and media examination to exclude a structural or deprivational cause
redFlags: An identifiable structural lesion (e.g. cataract, retinoblastoma, optic nerve disease) that could account for reduced vision and must not be attributed to amblyopia alone
Deprivation amblyopia from congenital cataract or dense media opacity requiring urgent intervention
Failure of vision to improve with adequate treatment, prompting re-evaluation for organic pathology
Poor vision persisting beyond the sensitive period with no prior treatment
reference.prognosis: The prognosis depends on the type of amblyopia and the age at which treatment begins; anisometropic and strabismic amblyopia treated early in childhood often recover good acuity, whereas deprivation amblyopia and late-treated cases have a more guarded outcome. Untreated amblyopia results in lifelong reduced vision in the affected eye and vulnerability if the better eye is later lost.
pitfalls: Diagnosing amblyopia without excluding a structural cause of visual loss
Delaying treatment beyond the sensitive period when response is greatly reduced
Failing to prescribe full refractive correction before or alongside occlusion therapy
Poor compliance with patching leading to treatment failure or reverse amblyopia in the occluded eye
management: Correct the underlying cause first, prescribing optical correction for refractive error and removing any deprivational cause such as urgent surgery for congenital cataract
Prescribe full cycloplegic refractive correction and allow a period of refractive adaptation, which alone may improve acuity
Treat residual amblyopia by penalising the better eye with occlusion patching to force use of the amblyopic eye
Use atropine penalisation of the sound eye as an alternative where patching adherence is difficult
Correct associated strabismus, with surgery where indicated for alignment
Begin treatment within the sensitive period, monitor acuity and adjust therapy while watching for reverse amblyopia in the treated eye
Support adherence with family education and maintain ophthalmology follow-up until vision stabilises
